# Session portability, targets, and community {#sec-session-portability}


- Make a greta model survive being saved and reloaded in a fresh R
  session, unblocking [targets](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/)
  pipelines - the single most-requested integration - and tidy up the
  ecosystem and community items that ride alongside it. Grouping
  labels: `targets-compat`, the `ecosystem` cluster, the `community`
  cluster.
- The core is one design (self-healing Python pointers) that also
  dissolves the model-cloning bug and the reloaded-plot bug; the rest
  are independent ecosystem conveniences.

**The problem.** Saving a greta model and reloading it in a fresh R
session breaks it, because the model holds pointers into a Python
session that no longer exists.

**The finding, code-verified.** Python handles do not live on greta
arrays or nodes - nodes store operation strings and plain R lists
(`R/node_types.R:120-122`, `R/node_class.R:6-7`); the Python session
is built on the dag by `new_tf_environment()` (`R/dag_class.R:73`).
And the dag *already contains the exact rebuild recipe*, today used
only for parallel chains: `define_tf_trace_values_batch()`
(`R/dag_class.R:44`) and `define_tf_log_prob_function()`
(`R/dag_class.R:50`). Re-running that recipe on a deserialised model is
expected to revive it - the same rebuild greta already performs on a
parallel worker's fresh Python session - and the
`saveRDS`->`callr`->rebuild round-trip below is the acceptance test
that will confirm it end-to-end.

**The fix** - the [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595)
design: wrap every access to a Python handle in a check that silently
rebuilds it if dead. This *replaces* the parallel-only special case at
`R/sampler_class.R:122-127` with one code path for parallel, targets,
and `saveRDS()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# new, R/dag_class.R: is a Python handle dead?
py_xptr_stale <- function(x) {
  is.null(x) || reticulate::py_is_null_xptr(x)
}

# new, R/dag_class.R: self-healing accessor -- the only way the
# log-prob function ever gets called
evaluate_log_prob_function = function(free_state) {
  if (py_xptr_stale(self$tf_log_prob_function)) {
    self$new_tf_environment()
    self$define_tf_log_prob_function()
  }
  self$tf_log_prob_function(free_state)
}
```

The predicate is named `py_xptr_stale()`, not `tf_stale()`, on purpose:
the question it asks - has this reticulate external pointer been
invalidated by a restarted Python session? - is a Python concern, not a
TensorFlow one, and is the identical check whichever backend (TF, JAX,
torch) computed the handle. It is a thin wrapper over reticulate's own
`py_is_null_xptr()`, so it borrows reticulate's `xptr` vocabulary and
stays out of greta's ~70-strong `tf_*` family, which are all TensorFlow
op wrappers rather than pointer predicates. Naming it this way keeps the
one piece of new session-portability machinery backend-neutral, in line
with the op-dictionary and backend-endgame work (milestone 11 and below).

The same pattern covers the sampler's `tf_evaluate_sample_batch`
(fixing sequential `extra_samples()` on reloaded draws) and the
`plot()` path ([#601](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/601)).
Acceptance test: round-trip a model and draws through `saveRDS()` into
a fresh R process via `callr`, then `mcmc()`, `extra_samples()`,
`calculate()`, and `plot()` all just work; plus a real
`targets::tar_script()` pipeline test, shipped with a "greta and
targets" vignette.


**What moved.** [#611](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/611)
(`greta_conflicts()`) and [#798](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/798)
(`value()` over a list) were written up here but are not about session
portability; both are now in milestone 3 with the rest of the greta
array semantics. Coming the other way,
[#701](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/701) - GitHub
Discussions versus the Discourse forum - used to sit outside the
milestone structure entirely, on the grounds that it is not package
code and so could not carry a version. Milestones no longer imply
versions, so it joins the community items it belongs with.

### [Issue #509](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/509)

- 2022-03-21
- Up Next
- MCMC crashes under `future::plan(cluster)` or `(multisession)`.
- problem: the parallel worker can't rebuild the model - the same dead-pointer cause as [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595).
- **does not reproduce — a candidate to close on the evidence below rather than to fix, and the framing must change.** Both `multisession` and `cluster` complete and return a valid 2-chain `greta_mcmc_list`. The reported `object 'tf' not found` is a 2022 report against TensorFlow 1.14 and greta's TF1 path. The parallel special case at `R/sampler_class.R:121-128` is precisely what makes it work today.
- so **[#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) does not *fix* a live parallel crash** — it lets that special case be deleted in favour of one self-healing path. That is a refactor win, not a bug fix, and the issue should be re-labelled accordingly. Step 2 of the fix document (explicit worker-side Python init) is **not needed for correctness**; workers initialise fine. Defensible as hardening, but do not sell it as required.
- **critical sequencing:** the fix document's step 3 deletes `R/sampler_class.R:122-127`. Doing that before [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595)'s step 4 covers `tf_evaluate_sample_batch` would **regress this issue from working to broken** — and since a dag-only rebuild demonstrably does not heal that handle, the risk is live, not theoretical. The acceptance test here is the right guard and must run in the same PR as the deletion.
- performance finding worth carrying: **`cluster` is ~18x slower than `multisession`** for identical work (126.6 s vs 7.1 s). Both correct, so not a bug, but plausibly each `cluster` worker re-initialises Python/TF per chain. Worth re-timing after [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) lands.
- proposed fix: see [fixes/issue-509.md](fixes/issue-509.md).
- priority: high (blocks parallel use).

### [Issue #557](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/557)

- 2022-10-03
- (none)
- Explore the {bundle} package for storing greta models.
- problem: {bundle} is the ecosystem's standard for serialising fitted models.
- **verdict: close as won't-fix, deferred until after [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595).** Tested against bundle 0.1.3 and greta 0.6.0 across two processes. `bundle()` on a greta model is a **silent no-op** today: no greta method exists, so `bundle.default` returns the object unchanged — same class, byte-identical serialised size (493332 both), and `unbundle()` returns something `identical()` to its input. The handle is still stale afterwards and `mcmc()` fails with the same dead-pointer error as plain `saveRDS`/`readRDS`. Users reaching for it get a false sense of safety.
- the categorical argument: `{bundle}` exists for models whose R object *cannot* be serialised meaningfully — keras (HDF5 weights blob), xgboost (external Booster pointer), h2o (JVM-hosted model). greta is not one of those. **greta's model *is* the R-side node graph, which `saveRDS` already captures**; the Python side is a derived cache, not state. That is demonstrable today — `plot()` and `calculate()` work on a reloaded model with no rehydration at all.
- after [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595), the method would wrap `identity()`: an S3 method, a `Suggests` dependency, conditional `.onLoad` registration and a test suite, all to add a second, competing answer to "how do I save a greta model?". The ecosystem argument is weak too — greta models are not `model_fit`/`workflow` objects and do not flow into vetiver pipelines.
- action: leave open until [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) lands, then close with a note pointing at the "greta and targets" vignette's `saveRDS` section. If a concrete vetiver-style workflow ever appears, it is a ~10-line adapter added then, against a real use case.
- proposed fix: [fixes/issue-557.md](fixes/issue-557.md) is technically accurate if implemented; the recommendation is that it should not be.
- priority: low (close, not build).
- defect in the proposed fix: the acceptance test in `fixes/issue-557.md` does not run. It builds on `distribution(as_data(rnorm(10))) <- normal(mu, 1)`, which parses but fails at runtime with *"target of assignment expands to non-language object"* - a replacement function needs an assignable name on the left, so the test fails at model definition, before reaching the behaviour under test. Assign first: `y <- as_data(rnorm(10))`, then `distribution(y) <- normal(mu, 1)`.

::: {.callout-important}
#### [#557](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/557) ({bundle}): close as won't-fix

This answers the question that sat unanswered here - *do we need
{bundle} at all once [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) is resolved?* **No.**

Tested against bundle 0.1.3 and greta 0.6.0 across two processes:
`bundle()` on a greta model today is a **silent no-op**. There is no
greta method, so `bundle.default` returns the object unchanged - same
class, byte-identical serialised size (493332 both), and `unbundle()`
returns something `identical()` to its input. The handle is still stale
afterwards and `mcmc()` fails with the same dead-pointer error as plain
`saveRDS`/`readRDS`. Users reaching for `bundle` today get a false sense
of safety, not a working model.

The categorical argument is the decisive one. `{bundle}` exists for
models whose R object *cannot* be serialised meaningfully - keras
(weights in an HDF5 blob), xgboost (external Booster pointer), h2o
(model on a JVM server). greta is not in that category: **greta's model
*is* the R-side node graph, which `saveRDS` already captures**, and the
Python side is a derived cache, not state. That is why `plot()` and
`calculate()` already work on a reloaded model with no rehydration at
all. After [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) lands, the `bundle` method would wrap `identity()` -
an S3 method, a `Suggests` dependency, conditional registration and a
test suite, all to add a second, competing answer to "how do I save a
greta model?".

**Action:** leave open until [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) lands, then close with a note pointing
at the "greta and targets" vignette's `saveRDS` section. If a concrete
vetiver-style workflow ever appears, it is a ~10-line adapter that can
be added then, against a real use case.
:::

### [Issue #595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595)

- 2023-11-15
- Up Next, impact-1
- Detect and "awaken" dead Python pointers so greta works with targets.
- problem: reloaded models point into a dead Python session.
- finding, code-verified: the rebuild recipe already exists (`R/dag_class.R:44,50,73`) and is applied only in the parallel branch (`R/sampler_class.R:122-127`).
- fix: add a `py_xptr_stale()` predicate and route every Python-handle use in `dag_class`/`sampler` through a self-healing accessor that rebuilds the tf environment on staleness, deleting the parallel-only special case at `R/sampler_class.R:122-127`; keep `awaken_greta_model()` as a now-optional wrapper.
- **the type assumption is verified, not assumed.** `self$tf_log_prob_function` — the return of `tensorflow::tf_function()` — has an S3 class vector terminating in `python.builtin.object`, exactly what `py_is_null_xptr()` requires. Across separate `Rscript` processes the predicate returns `FALSE` live and `TRUE` on a genuinely dead handle, and the rebuild recipe restores a working one. `is.null()` alone returns `FALSE` after reload (class attributes survive serialisation; only the pointer is nulled), so the `py_is_null_xptr()` arm **is required**. The predicate is also safe to call before Python is initialised.
- **step 4 is load-bearing, not optional.** A dag-only rebuild fixes `mcmc()` but leaves `extra_samples()` **broken** — that dead handle lives on the *sampler*, not the dag. Verified directly. Shipping steps 1-3 alone ships with `extra_samples()` still broken.
- **sequencing warning:** do not delete `R/sampler_class.R:122-127` before step 4 lands. That block is currently the only thing making parallel MCMC work, so deleting it early regresses [#509](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/509) from working to broken. The deletion and the sampler-side accessor must be in the same PR.
- scope correction: the fix document lists `R/calculate.R` and `R/greta_model_class.R` (plot) among files needing re-pointing. **Neither does** — both already work on a reloaded model. Harmless to include, but it inflates the estimate.
- proposed fix: see [fixes/issue-595.md](fixes/issue-595.md). All its `file:line` references were checked and are accurate.
- priority: high (headline of this milestone).

::: {.callout-note}
#### The [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) approach is sound - the type assumption was verified

This previously carried a warning that the whole design rested on an
unverified assumption: that `py_is_null_xptr()` would behave correctly
on `self$tf_log_prob_function`, which is the return of
`tensorflow::tf_function()` rather than a raw reticulate handle. **The
feared type mismatch does not exist.** That object's S3 class vector
terminates in `python.builtin.object`, exactly what
`py_is_null_xptr()` requires. Verified across separate `Rscript`
processes: the predicate returns `FALSE` on a live handle (no spurious
rebuilds) and `TRUE` on a genuinely dead one, and the rebuild recipe
restores a working handle. Note `is.null()` alone returns `FALSE` after
reload - class attributes survive serialisation and only the external
pointer is nulled - so the `py_is_null_xptr()` arm of the disjunction is
doing the real work and **is required**. Proceed as designed.

Two implementation caveats, both load-bearing:

1. **Step 4 is not optional.** A dag-only rebuild (steps 1-3) fixes
   `mcmc()` but leaves `extra_samples()` **broken**, because that dead
   handle lives on the *sampler* object, not the dag. Verified directly.
   A fix shipping only steps 1-3 ships with `extra_samples()` still
   broken.
2. **Do not delete `R/sampler_class.R:122-127` before step 4 lands.**
   That block is currently the *only* thing making parallel MCMC work.
   Deleting it first would regress
   [#509](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/509) from **working
   to broken**. Since a dag-only rebuild demonstrably does not heal
   `tf_evaluate_sample_batch`, this is a live risk, not a theoretical
   one: the deletion and the sampler-side accessor must land in the same
   PR, guarded by the parallel test.
:::

### [Issue #599](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/599)

- 2023-12-15
- Up Next
- greta listed in a targets workflow's `imports` should invalidate correctly.
- problem: targets change-tracking of greta objects.
- **does not reproduce, and the premise is inverted — a candidate to close on the evidence below rather than to fix.** Four real `targets` pipelines were run. With the awaken hook, `imports = "greta"` works *and* correctly skips on re-run; without it, `packages = "greta"` fails too, with a byte-identical error. The discriminating variable is not `imports` — it is plain [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595).
- finding: follows directly once [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) makes objects reload-safe, at which point *both* `packages` and `imports` work with no hook at all.
- fix: docs + integration test, **no code change**. Step 3 of the fix document (a stable session-independent hash to support `imports`) is **unnecessary** — `imports` already hashes stably and invalidates correctly. The `imports` variant of the acceptance test should be asserted to **pass**, not skip-documented.
- for the vignette rather than the tracker: `imports` re-runs cost **6.9 s vs 37 ms** for the skip check because targets hashes greta's whole namespace, and an identical model serialises to **1.70 MB under `imports` vs 493 kB under `packages`**. Both support the `packages` + `renv` recommendation on performance grounds alone.
- proposed fix: see [fixes/issue-599.md](fixes/issue-599.md).
- priority: medium (rides on [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595)).
- defect in the proposed fix: the acceptance test in `fixes/issue-599.md` does not run. It builds on `distribution(as_data(rnorm(10))) <- normal(mu, 1)`, which parses but fails at runtime with *"target of assignment expands to non-language object"* - a replacement function needs an assignable name on the left, so the test fails at model definition, before reaching the behaviour under test. Assign first: `y <- as_data(rnorm(10))`, then `distribution(y) <- normal(mu, 1)`.

### [Issue #601](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/601)

- 2024-01-16
- (none)
- Plotting a greta dag after reloading the model doesn't always work.
- problem: `plot()` touches a dead handle.
- **does not reproduce in any state constructible — but confirm with the reporter before closing.** `plot()` returned a valid `grViz` htmlwidget in all four states tested (first thing in a fresh session, after a failed `mcmc()`, after a hand-written awaken, and on a simple model), across two model shapes including one rich in operation nodes.
- finding: **not** a dead-pointer path at all. `plot.greta_model` (`R/greta_model_class.R:154`) touches only R-side structure — `adjacency_matrix` (pure R, `R/dag_class.R:809-816`), `names(node_list)`, `node_types`, `plotting_label()`, `visible_greta_arrays`. Nothing dereferences a Python handle, so there is no dead pointer for it to hit. The fix document's step 1 audit is already satisfied and its concern about guarding `adjacency_matrix` is unnecessary.
- caveat: the issue says plotting "doesn't *always* work" and the reporter's `example-greta-targets` setup was not reproduced verbatim. A missing DiagrammeR (`check_diagrammer_installed()`, `R/greta_model_class.R:155`) is a plausible alternative cause with nothing to do with dead pointers. **One round-trip with the reporter before closing.**
- fix: **write no code.** Land the acceptance test only — the `ok_plot` assertion folded into the [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595) `callr` round-trip. It passes against 0.6.0 today, which makes it a regression guard rather than a bug fix.
- proposed fix: see [fixes/issue-601.md](fixes/issue-601.md).
- priority: medium (rides on [#595](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/595)).
